title: Are Claude "skills" actually useful?
author: 710cartman
selftext:
[https://github.com/EL4CTEO/blender-skills](https://github.com/EL4CTEO/blender-skills)

[https://github.com/arjun988/blender-skills](https://github.com/arjun988/blender-skills)

Those are a couple of examples I came across, but are things like that actually useful? Anyone have experience with those, some some similar?  
  
I don't think they will be any replacement for constant iteration, precise prompts, and my strive for borderline perfection... but if those things could help optimize the process, that would be nice..

comments.author: CrowdGoesWildWoooo
comments.body:
Very much task dependent.

So just to give a brief on what Claude skills is, it’s basically an SOP, “if you see X, this is what you do”. 

It keeps things more predictable rather than let it run and do whatever he believe is correct. Sometimes an interaction is not in its training data so like if you already know how to do certain things, it’s better to just tell it rather than wasting tokens for it to try and discover how to tackle that problem.

comments.author: ProbablyDoesntLikeU
comments.body: Grill me yes. I build my own for anything else

replies.author: Evile_Gaming
replies.body:
Yes, Matt Pocock's dev skills are pretty nice, they keep things clean so you don't end up with a regression-ridden monolith of spaghetti code.

I also found it useful to iissu a standing order to the agent to build skills for successful workflows. It can save a lot of tokens to prevent re-inventing the wheel every time you ask for a deploy/commit or other repetitive workflows.

comments.author: _DCtheTall_
comments.body:
Skills are essentially prompts for your model context. They sometimes also add tools to the agent. What is useful about them is they are **reusable**.

Say you have a task you want Claude (or some other LLM agent) to do, but you need to give it specific instructions on formatting. You could type those instructions every time, but that wastes time. You could copy+paste between chats, but that is a brittle way to repeat tasks and also hard to transfer to new people.

Skills allow you to store these types of instructions in a way you can reuse them, others can reuse them, and if something in them needs to be changed then everyone gets the change in their future chats from updating the centralized skill.

There's nothing fancy about skills. They are for making prompts reusable.

comments.author: Luciferrrro
comments.body:
Skills are a must have, but the ones you create and rarely downloaded ones.  
Like if your are happy with what claude just did, for example model or game menu, then you write him to create a skill.

comments.author: Any-Blacksmith-2054
comments.body: I use more high-level skills; not just blender or godot but entire prompt/art/scenes/core mechanic process

comments.author: caesium23
comments.body: If you're using an agent without skills, you're basically just vibe coding.

comments.author: Altruistic-Spare9069
comments.body: My advice is to tell Claude to read the skill you are interested with and analyze it first as you might be shocked what kind of crap people are sharing , that can harm you non-intentionally but also intentionally

comments.author: lordcohliani
comments.body: Skills fill the gaps in your own prompting knowledge.
